citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to use appropriate methods to diagnose and treat an injury for one adult male ostrich, resulting in its
death on September 22, 2026.
According to the facility’s end of day record for September 14, 2026, staff noted that the male ostrich had a, “big cut/gash
on right leg,” and it was sprayed with Vetericyn. During the inspection, a facility representative showed the inspector a
picture of the ostrich’s wound from September 14 when it was first noticed. The wound in the picture was deep and
appeared multiple inches long, with red material coating the leg beneath it.
On September 16, 2026, the end of day record states, “ostrich cut still pretty bad, won’t let us get close.” On September
17, 2026, the end of day record states, “ostritch outback with cut was struggling to get up/limping a little.” On September
18, 2026, the end of day record states, “injured male ostritch is isolating himself,” and “male ostritch got Vetericyn (wound
is black from dried blood).” On September 20, 2026, the end of day record states, “injured ostrich isolating,” and “ostrich
sprayed vetracyn.” A veterinary report form dated September 22, 2026, stated, “the ostrich passed the next day, the vet
was contacted multiple times but never answered.” In the section describing the reason for veterinary contact, it states
that they did not think the cut was very deep so they sprayed it with Vetericyn and monitored the animal and it went
downhill very quickly. Based on the other records and the picture of the wound, this was not appropriate diagnosis or
treatment and signs that the animal was worsening were documented over the course of a week.
When the inspector spoke with the consulting veterinarian, the veterinarian stated that he had missed the facility’s call and
when he had called back the next day, he was told that the ostrich had already died. According to the facility
representatives, no other veterinarians, including the attending veterinarian, were contacted regarding the ostrich. When
reviewing the program of veterinary care, the only guidance stated that the facility was approved to use Vetericyn
products as a first aid but it does not have instructions for more serious injuries. The facility did not obtain veterinary
approval to treat an injury of this severity and did not change their treatment even as the ostrich continued to decline.
Failure to use appropriate methods to treat injuries or obtain veterinary care for an animal can lead to prolonged suffering
and death. Each exhibitor shall establish and maintain programs of adequate veterinary care that include the use of
appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries, and the availability of emergency,
weekend, and holiday care.
To be corrected from this day, October 9, 2026, forward.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
